prompt.context: Your client is a multinational pharmaceutical company. The client has a portfolio of drugs for major disease areas, including cancer, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal diseases. The client has experienced a decline in revenue over the last 18 months, and is fearful of further declines, especially given that its most commercially successful drug, which treats acid reflux, a gastrointestinal disease, will be going off patent in the next year.
prompt.question: What are the areas they should investigate to change the course of this trend?

clarifying_info.a: It is a multinational company — think of it like a GSK or AstraZeneca that operates around the world.

clarifying_info.q: What disease areas does the portfolio cover?
clarifying_info.a: Current disease areas include Neuroscience, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, and Cardiovascular. Each disease area has a portfolio of drug products.

clarifying_info.q: How does the business model work?
clarifying_info.a: Like a typical large pharmaceutical company: in-house R&D produces brand-name drugs that are sold through commercial sales teams, requiring doctor prescriptions through standard channels.
Generic companies will be new competitors as drugs go off patent.

exhibits.title: Company Revenues by Disease Area (in $B)
exhibits.shows: A table showing each drug, its disease area, its percentage of total 2021 revenue, and its year-over-year percentage change in revenue. Also shows total company revenue for 2020 and 2021.

data.note: Each drug does not make up the whole portion of Revenue by Disease Area

framework: Identify this as a revenue problem driven by product mix decline and imminent patent expiration
Product Mix: analyze revenue by disease area and by drug; identify winners and losers
Market & Industry Trends: assess competitive landscape, patent cliff dynamics, generic entry
Geographic Segmentation: break revenue down by region given the company is multinational
Growth Levers — Build / Buy / Partner: organic R&D pipeline, in-licensing or M&A, partnerships or co-promotion deals

questions.prompt: Review Exhibit 1. What are your key observations about the overall business and which segments are driving the decline?
questions.guidance: Overall revenue fell ~$2B (~9%) from $20B to $21B (approximated as $20B). Neuroscience (Green Pill, -33%) is the steepest percentage decliner. Cardiovascular (Red Pill) and Gastrointestinal (Purple Pill) are both down ~10%. Only Respiratory (Blue Pill) is growing (+10%) and gaining market share. The business is broadly deteriorating except in Respiratory.

questions.prompt: Which drug is the largest source of dollar declines from 2020 to 2021?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate 2021 revenue, back out 2020 revenue using the YOY % change, then compute the dollar decline for each declining drug. Green Pill has the largest dollar decline at ~$1B.

math.setup: Round total 2021 revenue to $20B. Use: 2021 Rev = $20B x (% of total); 2020 Rev = 2021 Rev / (1 - |% decline|); $ Decline = 2020 Rev - 2021 Rev
steps: Red Pill: 2021 Rev = $20B x 22% = $4B (rounded from 20%); 2020 Rev = $4B / 0.9 = $4.44B; Decline = $4.44B - $4B = $0.44B
Blue Pill is growing so no need to calculate decline
math.answer: Green Pill is the largest source of dollar declines at approximately $1B

questions.prompt: Given the Green Pill analysis, evaluate two options for the Purple Pill when it goes off patent next year. Option 1: Do nothing. Option 2: License the brand to an OTC manufacturer for a $1B one-time payment but accept 50% volume transfer to OTC. Assume current Purple Pill revenue is $3B at a 75% margin, and that without licensing the pill loses 1/3 of volume annually to generics (same as Green Pill). What is the gross profit for each option over 2 years, and which would you recommend?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a two-year gross profit table for each option. Do Nothing is better over the full two-year horizon ($2.5B vs $2.25B). A strong candidate also discusses the long-term trajectory: licensing accelerates volume loss and the brand retention benefit may not justify it unless cannibalization is minimal.

math.setup: Purple Pill 2021 revenue = $3B (rounded); margin = 75%; annual volume loss to generics = 1/3 per year
steps: Do Nothing Year 1: $3B x 2/3 = $2B revenue; $2B x 75% = $1.5B gross profit
Do Nothing Year 2: $2B x 2/3 = $1.33B revenue; $1.33B x 75% = $1.0B gross profit
License Year 1: $1B one-time fee + ($1.5B GP from Do Nothing / 2 due to 50% volume loss) = $1B + $0.75B = $1.75B gross profit
License Year 2: $0.5B gross profit (same as Do Nothing Year 1 halved: $1.0B / 2 = $0.5B)
math.answer: Do Nothing total GP = $2.5B; License total GP = $2.25B. Do Nothing is preferable on a two-year basis.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some issues that could have caused the Green Pill revenue decline?

categories.name: Pricing Pressure
ideas: Lower price per pill due to generic competition
Payer mix shift toward Medicaid or managed care with lower reimbursement rates

categories.name: Volume Decline
ideas: Lower tablet sales volume as generics enter
Generics coming on market taking share (confirmed as ~50% of the decline)
Out-of-stock or inventory-related issues (confirmed as contributing factor)

categories.name: Regulatory & Legal
ideas: Medicaid liability issues (confirmed as contributing factor)

categories.name: Market & Competitive
ideas: Changing prescribing habits or clinical guidelines
Geographic-specific trends (some markets more exposed to generic entry)

categories.name: Macro & Operational
ideas: Foreign currency headwinds in international markets

recommendation: Over the two-year horizon, 'Do Nothing' generates $2.5B gross profit vs. $2.25B for Licensing; recommend Do Nothing for the Purple Pill
The company should simultaneously pursue growth in Respiratory (Blue Pill), where it is gaining share, and explore in-licensing or M&A to replenish the pipeline in declining disease areas
risks: Licensing may preserve brand equity and over-the-counter presence long-term — relevant if the analysis extends beyond two years
Generic erosion may accelerate faster than the 1/3 annual assumption, compressing Do Nothing upside
Remaining pipeline may be insufficient to offset multiple patent cliffs across Neuroscience, Gastrointestinal, and Cardiovascular simultaneously
next_steps: Quantify the patent expiration timeline and revenue at risk for all drugs in the portfolio
Assess R&D pipeline depth and time-to-market for next-generation compounds
Evaluate geographic diversification — expand into emerging markets where generics have less penetration
Model licensing economics beyond two years and assess brand cannibalization rates before ruling it out entirely
